lessons.title: The 1970s Great Inflation: Oil Shocks, Wage-Price Spirals, and US Stagflation

children.text: Textbook economics of the 1960s taught that high inflation and high unemployment could not exist together. When demand runs hot, inflation rises but jobs are plentiful; when demand is weak, unemployment rises but so does the pressure on prices to fall. The 1970s broke that rule in the world's largest economy. Oil quadrupled almost overnight, wages and prices were frozen by government decree, and inflation and unemployment rose together for years. Economists needed a new word for it: stagflation.

body.text: Stagflation is not supposed to be possible in simple textbook models. The 1970s happened anyway, because a genuine cost-push shock met a central bank and a political system that kept treating an increasingly monetary problem as someone else's temporary bad luck.

events.title: The Nixon Shock
events.description: President Nixon ends the dollar's convertibility into gold, closing the Bretton Woods era, and imposes a 90-day freeze on wages and prices, later extended into phased controls through 1974.

events.title: The OPEC Oil Embargo
events.description: Arab oil-producing nations embargo the US and its allies after the Yom Kippur War. Crude oil prices roughly quadruple within months, a textbook cost-push shock hitting every importing economy at once.

events.title: The First Stagflation Recession
events.description: US CPI inflation peaks near 12% even as the economy slides into recession and unemployment climbs toward 9%, the first time inflation and joblessness had risen together on this scale.

events.title: The Wage-Price Spiral Entrenches
events.description: Union contracts with automatic cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) clauses spread widely, so wages rise automatically with CPI, feeding straight back into business costs and the next round of price increases.

events.title: The Second Oil Shock
events.description: The Iranian Revolution disrupts oil supply again, roughly doubling crude prices for the second time in the decade and pushing CPI inflation above 11%, on its way past 13% by 1980.

events.title: Volcker Takes Over
events.description: President Carter appoints Paul Volcker as Fed Chair, setting up the sharpest monetary policy turn of the era, the subject of the next lesson.

children.text: The Nixon Shock and the End of Bretton Woods

Under the post-war Bretton Woods system, the US dollar was pegged to gold and other major currencies were pegged to the dollar, giving the world a fixed-exchange-rate anchor. By 1971, persistent US deficits and rising doubts that America actually held enough gold to honour that promise put the system under strain. Nixon's response, closing the gold window, effectively let the dollar float and removed the last hard external constraint on how much money the US could create. The wage-price freeze announced the same week was meant to control inflation directly, but freezing prices without controlling the money supply behind them does not remove inflationary pressure, it just hides it, and sets up a sharper burst once the controls are eventually lifted.
The 1973 Oil Embargo: A Textbook Cost-Push Shock

The October 1973 embargo is the cleanest cost-push case study in modern history. Crude oil went from roughly $3 a barrel to around $12 a barrel within a few months, a shock that hit transport, manufacturing, heating and food costs across every oil-importing economy simultaneously, with no change in domestic demand required to explain it. This is the engine from Chapter 1 in its purest form: an input cost shock, not a credit boom or a demand surge, doing the damage.

body.title: US CPI Inflation, 1970-1982: Two Humps, One Decade

children.text: The Wage-Price Spiral: When the Cure Becomes the Cause

A single oil shock should, in principle, fade once supply adjusts. What turned the 1970s into a full decade of high inflation was the wage-price spiral you met as a flashcard term in the last chapter, now playing out at national scale. Large numbers of American union contracts carried cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) clauses, automatically raising wages in line with CPI. That protected workers' purchasing power in the short run, but it also meant every oil-driven price spike fed straight into the next round of wage costs, which businesses then passed on as higher prices, which triggered the next COLA adjustment. The mechanism that was meant to protect households from inflation became a channel that kept renewing it.

body.title: Trace the Spiral
body.scenario: A US auto workers' union contract includes a COLA clause: wages rise automatically by the same percentage as the prior year's CPI increase. Oil prices spike, pushing CPI up 8% for the year. The following year, autoworker wages rise 8% under the COLA clause, and the auto manufacturer raises car prices to cover the higher labour cost.
body.prompt: Walk through what happens in year three if oil prices stay flat but this wage-price mechanism keeps running. Does the spiral need a fresh oil shock to continue, or can it become self-sustaining, and what does that imply about how hard it becomes to stop?
body.modelAnswer: The spiral can become self-sustaining without any further oil shock. Year three's CPI reading will already be elevated because car prices (and other goods across the economy following the same COLA logic) rose in year two, which triggers another round of COLA-driven wage increases in year three, which again gets passed through as higher prices. The original oil shock only had to happen once; the wage-price mechanism, once entrenched across enough of the economy, keeps the inflation running under its own momentum. This is precisely why 1970s inflation proved so stubborn and why breaking it, as the next lesson covers, required deliberately causing a recession severe enough to break the expectation that wages and prices would keep chasing each other upward.

body.text: Fed Chair Arthur Burns, under documented political pressure from the Nixon White House ahead of the 1972 election, largely treated 1970s inflation as a cost-push problem beyond the Fed's control, an outside shock rather than something monetary policy had allowed to take root. That framing kept interest rates lower than the inflation numbers arguably warranted for most of the decade, letting inflation expectations drift upward and become self-fulfilling, exactly the outcome the wage-price spiral above describes.

body.label: The Misery Index
body.context: A simple measure popularised in this era, the misery index topped 20 by 1980, and became a political weapon used against both Presidents Ford and Carter.

body.text: Keep this decade in mind for Chapter 4. In 2021, central banks around the world, including the US Fed, initially called a fresh round of inflation "transitory", a supply-side, pandemic-driven shock that would fade on its own. The 1970s is exactly why that word made economists nervous: the first oil shock of 1973 also looked transitory at first, right up until a wage-price spiral made it structural.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: What made the 1970s Great Inflation unusually difficult to fight compared with a pure demand-pull boom?
options: Interest rates had no effect on inflation during this period
A cost-push oil shock became entrenched through a wage-price spiral, so inflation kept running even without repeated fresh shocks
The US government banned all interest rate changes during the 1970s
Oil prices fell continuously throughout the decade, confusing policymakers
body.explanation: A pure demand-pull boom responds fairly directly to higher interest rates cooling spending. The 1970s were harder because an initial cost-push shock got locked in by COLA-driven wage-price dynamics, so the inflation became self-sustaining and required a much larger, more painful policy response to break, which is the story of the next lesson.

points: The 1970s combined a genuine cost-push shock, the 1973 and 1979 oil embargoes, with monetary and political choices that let inflation become entrenched rather than fade.
Nixon's 1971 closing of the gold window and wage-price freeze removed a monetary anchor while masking rather than solving inflation, setting up a sharper burst later.
The wage-price spiral, wages and prices chasing each other upward through mechanisms like COLA clauses, can make inflation self-sustaining even after the original shock has passed.
The Fed under Arthur Burns largely treated this as an external, cost-push problem beyond its control, which let inflation expectations drift upward for most of the decade.

This is the direct historical reason the word "transitory" makes economists nervous, and it sets up why breaking the 1970s spiral eventually required the deliberately brutal response covered in the next lesson.
